reasoning: The extract commits to evaluation but does not say what will be measured or how. Several lines promise a further review before legislating, to consider "the latest life expectancy projections" and "evaluate the effects of current rises in State Pension age". One line gives a timetable: the next review is "to be conducted by July 2023" and will "confirm when State Pension age will increase to 68". Another says the Government "will analyse the impact of changes to State Pension age already in train", naming the equalisation to 65 and the rise to 66, and says this will "provide additional evidence". A further line says the Government will "monitor the effects of State Pension age rises alongside" reforms to pensions, welfare and the labour market. Impact assessment material is promised "at the appropriate time". This gives some indication of evaluation intent and a timetable, so it exceeds level 0 and 1. It falls short of level 2 because no success measures or outcomes are named, no method is described, and no testing is discussed. The one citation (Reference 42, DWP benefit expenditure tables) supports a spending figure and is not an evaluation plan. The strongest counter-example to level 1 is the dated July 2023 review and the stated aim of analysing past rises, which look like a plan with a timetable. But it is a review of life expectancy and prior rises, not a defined way of measuring whether the policy worked. To reach level 2 the document would need to name the outcomes to be measured (for example employment, health, benefit claims or poverty among those affected), and set out how the evaluation of earlier rises will be done. Level 3 would also require explaining why, and saying when and where results will be published.
